items.title: Finite populations and sampling designs
items.statement: Defines a nonempty finite population with fixed real values, its total and mean, a probability mass function on sampled subsets, design expectation, first- and second-order inclusion probabilities, the observed-record experiment, and the distinction from a superpopulation model.
items.strategy: Definition: state the finite index set, fixed values, sample support and weights, targets, inclusion events, design expectation, common observed-record space and induced laws; use the required unit and fixed/random conventions.

items.title: A finite-population design induces probability laws on observed records
items.statement: For each fixed population-value function y, the observed-record set function induced by a finite sampling design is a probability measure on the common full-power-set record space.
items.strategy: Direct: verify the full power set is a sigma-algebra, the induced set function has total mass one, and finite support makes it countably additive.

items.title: The Horvitz–Thompson total and mean are design-unbiased under positive inclusion probabilities
items.statement: For a fixed finite population and a declared finite sampling design with pi_i>0 for every unit, the estimator sum over sampled units of y_i/pi_i is unbiased for the total; division by the population size gives an unbiased estimator of the finite-population mean.
items.strategy: Direct: apply finite expectation linearity to the finite sum of inclusion indicators and use the indicator-expectation identity.

items.title: A zero inclusion probability prevents total identification and universal unbiased estimation
items.statement: If some unit has zero first-order inclusion probability, two finite populations differing only at that unit have the same observed-data law and different totals. Thus the total is not identifiable, and no estimator based only on the observed sample can be unbiased for every finite population.
items.strategy: Direct: change one never-observed population value, compare the observed records pointwise, then use equal estimator expectations to contradict unbiasedness for both totals.

title: Finite populations and design probability — Examples

items.title: SRSWOR inclusion probabilities, pairwise nonpositive indicator covariance, and the sample mean
items.statement: For uniform sampling of n-subsets from N fixed units with N>=2 and 1<=n<=N, computes first- and second-order inclusion probabilities, the covariance of distinct inclusion indicators, and the Horvitz–Thompson mean as the usual sample mean.
items.strategy: Count unit/sample incidences and ordered-pair/sample incidences by symmetry; expand the covariance from its definition and specialize the Horvitz–Thompson estimator.

items.title: A certainty unit and a census under Horvitz–Thompson estimation
items.statement: A three-unit design that always samples one unit gives its Horvitz–Thompson contribution without expansion; a census makes every inclusion probability one and the Horvitz–Thompson total and mean exact.
items.strategy: Compute the inclusion probabilities and estimator for the two-sample certainty-unit design, then evaluate the single-outcome census design.

items.title: An unobserved unit prevents universal unbiased estimation
items.statement: When the design always samples unit 1 from a two-unit population, two populations with different totals produce the same observed record, so every observed-sample estimator has the same expectation under both.
items.strategy: Write the degenerate design law and two population schedules explicitly; compare their inclusion probabilities, records, totals, and estimator expectations.
